header.source: Translated by Claude (claude-opus-5-5, Anthropic) from the library's tlg2200.tlg00517.opp-grc1, from Open Greek and Latin's First1KGreek (CC BY-SA 4.0), one English line for each line of the original. notes.urn:cts:greekLit:tlg2200.tlg00517.opp-gr: Section 2: the printed text has the edition's manuscript sigla (Ath, P, H, Ma, D) intruded into the line; these are omitted, and the sentence read as ending παρ' ὑμῶν. Section 6 (ref 3.4): κρίνεται δὲ ἕκαστος ἐκ τοῦ μισθοῦ τῶν γραφόντων is obscure; 'by the pay of those who draft [decrees]' is tentative. The doubled καὶ καὶ in the same line is taken as a dittography. Section 7: τριταγωνισταὶ and γραφεῖς τυμπάνων are jibes at Aeschines' acting career and family background. ὧς is read as ὡς throughout.

17: <τις> is an editorial supplement; rendered 'anyone at all'. 18.1: the clause 'τὸ δυνάμενον <ἂν> εἴ τις λόγος γενναῖος' is difficult and probably corrupt; the rendering is tentative. 31.1: the text breaks off after 'κομί-' (κομίζεσθαι); a lacuna follows, marked [...]. 27.1: 'τἀριοτείδου' read as τἀριστείδου (Aristides).

33: the antecedent of 'those [places]' is loose; sense uncertain. 35: the words from 'You yourselves installed…' are taken as the imagined retort of other Greeks; there are no quotation marks in the Greek. 38: 'Κρεῖττον γὰρ ἦν, φησίν, <ἢ>' is lacunose; 'it was too strong' is a conjectural sense. 'ὅσ’ ἁ προσῆκεν' is read as ὅσα προσῆκεν. 43: the text is lacunose ('βαρον' read as βάρβαρον); '[do not admit]' is supplied for the sense. 44: 'ὁ φόβος γε τοῦ λυσιτελεῖν σφισιν' seems corrupt; probably a negative is missing ('lest it not profit'). The rendering is tentative. 46: 'the throne, the scimitar' presumably refer to Xerxes' silver-footed throne and Mardonius' scimitar dedicated on the Acropolis. 47: 'ἴ’' is read as ὦ.

47.2: the last sentence may be meant as a question ("did you not fear then...?"). 50.1: the text reads "πα- ἀρχήν· ἀρχήν" with "λοτιμεῖσθαι"; read as "τὴν παροῦσαν ἀρχήν" and "φιλοτιμεῖσθαι". 55.1: "ἵππαρχοι δὲ φίλοι καὶ ταξίαρχοι" is obscure and possibly corrupt; translated literally. 57.1: ΙΙνδναῖοι read as Πυδναῖοι (Pydnaeans). 61.1: stray "ἱν." after Ἀθήνησιν is a duplication and omitted. 63.1: the final sentence (εἱστήκει ... ἐκ τῶν ... ἀποφευγόντων) is syntactically difficult; the rendering is uncertain.

64.1: 'πρὶν οὓς ἄξιον ὑμᾶς ἰδεῖν αὐτὸν ὑπισχνούμενος' looks corrupt or lacunose; rendering is tentative. 67.1: the clause 'ὅτε τοῦτον ἐμνημόνευσαν, ὑπῆλθον δουλείας ζυγόν' is obscure; translated loosely as the heralds proposing slavery. 68.1: 'ἥγ’ εἷται' read as ἡγεῖται. 70.1: 'ὅ τι ναιντο' read as ὅ τι δύναιντο; Acragallidae are the tribe linked with Cirrha in the First Sacred War. 73.1: Atrestidas, the Arcadian said to have received Olynthian captives from Philip. 77.1: identity of Callias uncertain (possibly Callias of Chalcis). 78.1: the final words are an editorial supplement, and the sentence seems incomplete.

Line 81.1: θεραπεύοιντο with ταύτης is ambiguous; taken as 'in the greatness of the enemy' (they would be courted by a powerful Philip). 'Fresh-kneaded cakes and figs' echoes Demosthenes' gibe (De Corona) at Aeschines' role in his mother's rites. Line 84.1: the Parnassus rockfall refers to the legend of the god's defence of Delphi against the Persians (or the Gauls). Jason of Pherae was assassinated by seven young men before the Pythian games of 370 BC.

nodes.text: XVII.
Aeschines, sent alone as *pylagoras* [delegate to the Amphictyonic Council], did not speak against Philip when he was being made an Amphictyon, and on his return he is tried for public wrongs.

It was not enough, it seems, for this Aeschines to open Thermopylae to Philip and to hand over to him a people as great as that of the Phocians; in addition to that earlier deed, he also brought it about that the Macedonian should become master of the affairs of the Amphictyonic assembly and one of the race of the ancient Amphictyons.

To me it does not seem remarkable that this man has made some part of Philip's affairs go better, but that among you it is very easy for a wrongdoer not to pay the penalty, and, while profiting at your expense, to be trusted by you again with other matters. And now the hard thing is not to show that the city has been gravely harmed by Aeschines, but to persuade you to hate those who serve the enemy against you. This is what makes most of those who are able to indict and to refute [such men] hesitate.

For my part, I would wish you to be pained by what has been done and to feel as those who have suffered such things may be expected to feel; but if, from having borne many wrongs, you bear this one too, at least I shall have kept my duty to the city. And once again it will become clear that one man was seen handing the villain over to judgement, but the matter was ruined by the negligence of the judges.

4. Now if the present inquiry happened to be held in the Amphictyonic assembly, the contest would not be on equal terms for me and for this man, with Philip judging in place of the Phocians and his bodyguards standing around; for clearly Aeschines' speeches, even with nothing strong in them, would have been able to win approval, while I, even speaking most justly of all, would have met uproar and much laughter from every side, if I had not been able to see even this much, that I had dared to prosecute Aeschines just where he is stronger. But since the trial is at Athens, and you have come into court according to the laws of Solon, and the danger is great if the oaths are disregarded, perhaps some gain may come to the city from this indictment: that this man may pay the penalty for both, both for the harm he did as ambassador and for the losses he caused as *pylagoras*, and that it may become clear to those who have emulated him that for those who take [money] from the enemy their daring ends in the utmost disaster.

5. That Aeschines has come into court having thought things over and having rehearsed long and persuasive speeches, I myself am not unaware, and I think you know it too; for when a man fears for his safety, and his deeds are wicked, and there is not a single straightforward argument on their behalf, he must of necessity be prepared to mislead the judges by whatever means he can. But you yourselves, when he does this, must be all the angrier and take it hard, if, being a craftsman of speech and full of every kind of sophistry, and having countless fine starting-points for speeches against the enemy of the city and of all the Greeks, he neither said nor uttered anything, but uses his art against the citizens, wronging the same people and trying to persuade them that they have not been wronged. So, if he is at a loss for words, as one unable even to brazen it out because of how evident his wrongs are, let him die; and if he spins out well-contrived speeches on behalf of such terrible deeds, then let him be convicted on that ground, for having hidden his ability in the Amphictyonic assembly.

6. Aeschines here, then, is the defendant, and the indictment has been brought against one man, the silent *pylagoras*; but you too, men of the jury, do not escape the same charge. In saying "you" I mean the people, who, as if in night and darkness, have been deprived of the power to discern what kind of man each of the citizens is. And the good man has been thought bad, the wretch decent, the just man wicked, and the best man the worst. Then the man who does not trouble you or rebuke you is quickly cast aside, while the bold and reckless man, <boasting> that he will have what he wants even against your will, is honoured and great and manages your affairs both in the city and in the Amphictyonic assembly, and each man is judged by the pay of those who draft [decrees], not by the life he has lived.

Hence those from families devoted to the people, and of whose goodwill there is the most testimony, are all but unknown, while third-rate actors and sailors and drum-painters speak, propose decrees, go on embassies, serve as generals, and act as *pylagoras*. The error made in the assemblies shows itself a little later, and, what is most terrible, you have not even noticed this while suffering it.

Here is proof: while the Phocians were still lamenting, while the wretched people were still being scattered from their cities, some fleeing, some being slaughtered, some feeding Macedonians, and while you laid the blame for the evils there on this one man, and some were shouting in the marketplace that it was not Philip's arms that destroyed the cities but the hopes that persuaded the people to sit still and to accept the decree threatening the Phocians, while, I say, men were saying such things and were convinced of them, the time of the Amphictyonic assembly came, demanding the goodwill of a speaker.

9. How then did we, the stricken ones, [fare]? Or rather, [to begin] a little further back: Philip had gained one great advantage, such as he had never had before since he came to power, to master Thermopylae and to scatter the people that stood as a bulwark for those within Thermopylae. Having achieved this quickly and easily by treaty, not by arms, thanks to this man, who persuaded [us] to trust instead of being on guard, he seeks a second [advantage], greater than the first: to share in the administration of the Amphictyonic assembly in place of those who had perished, and to partake in the name and standing of the Amphictyons.

Now the Thessalians, and some others of those who had long since learned to make shameful gains, would, he thought, receive him most gladly and judge him a more genuine Amphictyon than the Phocians; and of the rest, those who did not like to see this would groan quietly, except for us; we alone, as though our own constitution were being disturbed, would oppose him, cry out, and thrust back the man attacking the institutions of the Greeks.

So, to prevent this, he arranges for an Athenian who resembled the Thessalians, one who would do him this favour and would eagerly open the second [door] for him too, to come from us to the Amphictyonic assembly. This took no great effort: someone came forward, well ahead of the others, and said, "Let us entrust the business of the Amphictyonic assembly to Aeschines." Those who had been primed applauded; of the rest, one did not even pay attention, another did not suspect, another was in a hurry to leave, another did not care about public affairs, and the one who spoke against it was a nuisance.

Why say more? What Philip wanted was voted by the Athenians. And from here went a *pylagoras* far more useful to him than Parmenion. For Parmenion would not persuade, since he would seem ready to gratify his master; but when someone from among the wronged works together with the one who has hurt them, he can do the greatest service, since his words arouse no suspicion.

So when this man came gladly through Phocis and saw the *hieromnemones* [the sacred delegates] and Philip, he showed the former, as one would expect, that he feared the man, so that if anyone happened to be confident, he might be cowed and give way; but with Philip himself he conversed and agreed on what was to happen and what the pay for it would be. And when Philip, as one would expect, said that he was rich and able to give, he arranged the rest in the way that was going to benefit him.

Those, then, who knew Aeschines well were calling Philip an Amphictyon even before the vote, for [they knew] he would do what he has done; but those who judged the *pylagoras* by the character of the city said: "In vain does this Philip lay hold of a share in the council. For the man who will not allow or permit it, but will strike back and block those of the Greeks who err, is close by: an Athenian, of a free city, one that cares for its race and protects the dignity of Greece."

These things they surmised as befitting an Athenian, but far from the bribe-taking of Aeschines, as was at once shown. For when the Amphictyons were in session, and the Thessalians and Thebans, who had long since disgraced themselves, had praised Philip at length, and had accused at length the Phocians who were no more, and finally had said that he must indeed be given a share in the council, as a king far better than the Phocians and more entitled to hold their votes, it was to be expected that at this our *pylagoras* would protest, call the heroes to witness, invoke the Pythian god at Pytho, and fill everything with shouting, rebuking, reproaching, accusing, shutting the council against the barbarian. But what does he do, and how did he honour the vote you gave him?

Go up, Aeschines, and tell the jurors the speeches on behalf of the common body of the Greeks which the people of the Athenians made through your voice. You are at a loss and bend your head to the ground. But then, at least, there was no lack of words for a man who was just, a friend of the Greeks, and an honour to those who sent him, in the causes he chose.

But how did he stand in silence, men of Athens, hearing such speeches, at which anyone at all would have cried out? He was voiceless while the Amphictyonic assembly was being seized, voiceless while the most sacred things were thrown into confusion, voiceless while the ordinance was being undermined, while such drunken outrage was borne in upon the council, and while the purest of the fine things among the Greeks was about to be defiled by mingling with barbarians. He, an Athenian, if indeed he is one, a *pylagoras*, badly chosen, but sent all the same, appointed to safeguard the city's interests with his judgement and his voice, as if he were some Persian or Scythian who had come from somewhere outside, to whom the overturning of our <customs> mattered little, thus uttered nothing, neither small nor greater, nor so much as grunted, like a slave whose master stands over him and orders him to be silent. So much, men of Athens, can gold do, given or expected.

Once the ill-minded and corrupted party had prevailed, the party that could have refused to tolerate anything shameful, if any noble word [had been spoken], followed along too. As it was, seeing the man from the greatest and most famous city standing by Philip in the council in silence, they thought it great folly to claim a higher spirit than you. Philip becomes an Amphictyon in place of the wretched Phocians. And this he buys from that man as his second purchase, or rather his third: Thrace, Phocis, the Amphictyonic assembly. And if you go to that place according to the ancient law, you will see the son of Amyntas managing the affairs of the Greeks.

19. So, having disposed of the Amphictyonic seat in this way, and having ruined a splendour confirmed over a long time, Aeschines himself would know what he received for it; but he has come here grown more haughty, and, though he perceives that his <opponents> are indignant, he is not afraid; and when his friends tell him to be afraid, since they know that what he has done is intolerable, he laughs.

And this, men of Athens, is naturally so. For when a man living here has his security not from living according to the laws but from the friendship of tyrants, then as long as things go well for them, these men too can be confident. So, together with those they serve, they also make their own affairs greater than the laws.

He is so bold, then, that he even says he has done you no wrong at all. For he has not, he says, taken from you an allied city, or land, or harbours, or revenues, or a wall; no, nor has he expelled the city from the Amphictyony, nor in any way at all made your position worse.

I could wish this statement of yours were true, Aeschines, and that none of our affairs were worse off because of your policy. For then Thrace and Cersobleptes, an ally and friend, would have been saved for me; and the Phocians, the adversaries of the Thebans, would have been saved, and many walls and arms and men, and a place that tips the balance greatly. But as it is, even if you die three times, you still owe a penalty.

23. But concerning those matters I shall prove [my case] at the audit of the embassy, and these men will be angry then; that they have now also been wronged in common, by the betrayal of the Amphictyonic assembly, the argument is very clear and short. Do not list for me a mass of wrongs for which I have not brought you to court, so as to steal away the charge on which you are being tried; but if you show that this is not a wrong, you may be acquitted, and if you cannot, what do you gain if you do not do wrong in every way? For these men are not accustomed to feel and acknowledge gratitude for not having been wronged in every respect, but to exact a penalty for having been wronged in any way whatever, since they also know how to repay gratitude to those who do them good, even if they prove to be benefactors in only one way.

If this were not so recognised among all mankind, both punishment and gratitude would have been removed from human life, since no one is able to do good or harm through every kind of good and evil deed. What, then, is the just limit of a defence? That a man charged with having killed should show that he did not kill, or that he killed justly; a man charged with betrayal, demonstrate that he did not betray; a man charged with striking, that he did not strike; a man charged with stealing, that he did not steal.

So too, then, with the present matter. You were sent, Aeschines, as *pylagoras*. You came to the Amphictyonic assembly. You found a barbarian being introduced into the secret things of the Greeks against the laws. You kept silent, though you had a tongue and knew how to speak. This is the wrong we say the city has suffered. Refute this charge, then. Leave the walls and places and harbours aside for now. For you stand convicted on this: of having lost by your silence the reputation the city possessed.

How much this is worth to the Athenians one could judge by considering for oneself that we distributed grain in the beginning, sent out our many colonies, buried the dead who were being wronged, received people in misfortune, and at Marathon dispelled the common danger of the Greeks, not so that for each of these we should get money from those who benefited and the city should grow rich, but so that we might hear what is more honourable than great wealth, 'fathers and nurturers of the race', and so that the poets might sing of Athens; and indeed they did sing, calling the city the bulwark of Greece.

Where, then, is the bulwark? How can this title be ours, a fine and lofty one, proclaiming our excellence more exactly than any crown, when we keep quiet amid the misfortunes of the Greeks and stay silent while present at the outraging of the most important things? For no one will say 'Aeschines kept silent', nor will he look for the name of the *pylagoras*, nor fix the blame on him; but he will refer the baseness of the man sent to the city, just as, I think, people call the merits of those who do some good the common merits of the city, such as those of Aristides, of Conon, of Themistocles. So now too [they will say]: the Athenians, seeing Philip become an Amphictyon, allowed it, received him, and thought those bringing him in were well-minded.

28. He says that what was done is a light matter and does the city no harm. But, Aeschines, different things grieve different people more: the Thessalians, for instance, not getting something, just as, I think, the Athenians [are grieved by] suffering loss of reputation. You would have been more moderate even now if you had betrayed places and harbours. The best thing, indeed, is to wrong one's native land neither in this way nor in that nor at all; but if a nature that is wicked drags a man down and the scoundrel cannot be sensible, let him do harm in other respects and keep his hands off its reputation.

I am so far from bearing the present matter calmly because the city has not been harmed in other respects that, even if Aeschines had happened to win us land and allies and revenues along with the present disgrace, I would not be any less angry at the wrongs done to us. And this I have been taught by the laws which our fathers laid down, not by writing them, as Solon and Draco did, but by acting, and handing down to us their deeds to imitate.

30. To go through everything is impossible; but, a thing no length of time could make one forget, the Persian once came against us leading Asia and the greater part of Europe. When he had overwhelmed the few Lacedaemonians at Thermopylae with his many, and was marching on our land, the Athenians of that time abandoned the land and held the sea in place of the city. And he was defeated at sea by those whose city he was razing. Thinking that they could not be taken by battle, but perhaps by gifts, he was ready to give some things and give back others: to give back land and city, and to give untold wealth, rule over the Greeks, and the friendship of the master of Asia.

How, then, did the men of that time take hearing this? They considered it all harm, and would not accept recovering their own property in this way. [...] And you must now show that we too have suffered no harm in this. But you could not. So you are rightly impeached.
32. Come, then, let us show that he is guilty of all the very harms he says he has not done.

That Philip, having already taken from the city places and cities and anchorages and money and captives and much else, came to such a pitch of insolence as even to drag off triremes from Marathon, no one at all is unaware; and that by sharing in the Amphictyony he would be less likely to let the Greeks be stirred up against him, being present, sitting in council with them, and now persuading, now threatening, now contradicting, now promising, this too is beyond dispute.

So the man who has made sure that what he would have lost, had he not obtained this last thing, will remain securely his, how could he not have robbed us of many places and many positions? For he might reasonably be thought to have given away those [places] that would have gone over to you, and to have taken from you those that will now stay with him.

And the harm is not only that of the time past, nor has Philip gained only so much as no longer to fear for what he acquired by wrongdoing. He will keep these [gains] as they are, and through this fine share in the council he will be still safer and greater, bringing his arms and his siege engines against those not yet subdued, while he will no longer have men in the Amphictyonic assembly stirring [it] up against him. For a king and tyrant is fearsome everywhere, not only when he makes war, but also when he sits in judgement and in council. Which of the wronged would lament what he has suffered, when Philip holds votes, is flattered, and persuades the common body of whatever he wishes? So the man who will not be content with what he has, but will always desire something more, and will force those who suffer to keep silent: are we to say that he has gained something from Aeschines' wicked silence, or not?

We have been accustomed, men of Athens, to send envoys and to cry out against Philip, and this has benefited the city more than a few times: embassies, speeches, accusations, and the 'Rouse yourselves!' and the 'He alone is the enemy of the Greeks.' Do you think, then, that it is still possible to go on such embassies? It is not. For who will put up with it? Who will pay attention? Who will not think the thing a riddle? 'You yourselves installed this perjured scoundrel, this enemy of the freedom of the Greeks, in the Amphictyonic assembly without difficulty, and did not let fall a single word against [it], plainly [taking him to be] honest and just and worthy of honours. Are you then not ashamed to speak ill now of the man you did not hold back when he was obtaining the greatest things?' So, after this, the whole people must necessarily imitate Aeschines' unnecessary silence, and no longer bring charges against the man who has done so much wrong?

And yet what price would Philip ever have paid for this: that no one from you should any longer go to the cities to expose his crimes, but that those who promote his interests in each place should enjoy a conspicuous absence of opponents? Is there, then, anyone so simple that you can persuade him that the same thing is to the advantage of both us and Philip? It cannot be; but just as what profits the city is distasteful to him, so what helps Philip is an obstacle and a harm to us.

37. 'For I saw,' he says, 'that the Amphictyons were set on it and had resolved to do [him] the favour.' This, then, is the very reason you ought to have spoken against it: that they were set on it and somewhat stirred up. If they had happened to have nothing of the kind in mind, then, being sensible men, they would not even have needed someone to restrain them. The horseman will check his horse when it runs to excess, but when it keeps to the measure he will not fight it by hauling on the bridle. Sick bodies need drugs, but healthy ones the doctor will look on from afar. Let the *pylagoras* [delegate to the Amphictyonic Council] too be a doctor when the Amphictyons are sick. For this is why he is sent: to put a stop to errors by speech. But you let the disease grow strong in the council.

38. 'For it was too strong,' he says. And from what knowledge do you say this, that they were incurable? If, having heard all that was fitting and a speech powerful enough to check their impulse, they had stayed where they were, you would have clearly proved what you claim; but if, while you kept silent, they became no better, what sign is that that they would have erred just the same even after speeches?

Great is the power, men of Athens, of the nature of speech, great. It has lulled civil strife to sleep and abolished war, striking the weapons from men's hands; it has soothed the angry, quenched grief, stopped tears; it has persuaded those who delight in quiet that war is better than peace, and those who shudder at the surgeons' incisions to offer their bodies bravely to the steel.

Croesus thought he should build ships and attack the islands, but when Bias showed him that it was not to his advantage, he gave up the voyage. We and the Thebans once drew up for battle, and when we were about to use our spears, the Corinthians appeared as mediators, and we went away before any wounds. The Mytilenaeans were thought to have done the city the gravest wrong in the war against the Peloponnesians, and the people of the Athenians, the gentlest of peoples, came to such a pitch of anger that a decree carried the day to destroy the city, all those of age, and a trireme was sailing carrying this [decree]. A second assembly, and a more reasonable speech by Diodotus, and decree was undone by decree.

And why must I say much? Even now you often go up to the assemblies desiring one thing, and go away having voted another, as reasoning overtakes your desires. What wonder, then, that the Amphictyons should have wanted the worse course, but, once they learned the harm in what they wanted, should have ratified the better?

42. This, Aeschines, is how one must use cleverness of speech: against enemies, on behalf of what is just; before the other Greeks on behalf of all the Greeks, not, by Zeus, against allies on behalf of barbarians, nor in the assemblies to deceive citizens; and above all to honour justice everywhere, but if one must somewhere use sophistry too, where one might gain the advantage over enemies, that is the moment for tricks.

But you had no need of sophistries or of elaborate speeches, Aeschines; you had an abundance of just arguments, with which even a private citizen could without difficulty have thrust Philip out: 'Men of the Amphictyony, this business is utterly outrageous. You are trampling on ancient oaths, confounding honoured customs, disturbing old laws laid down by men dear to the gods, who are said to have lived at the time of that extraordinary flood. O Earth and Pythian [Apollo], will those who [do not admit] even Greeks outside the list accept a tyrant and a barbarian?' Did you not know this? Was this not the easiest thing to say? Did you not know that the number is fixed to certain peoples? Ionians, Dorians, Boeotians, Perrhaebians, Magnesians, Achaeans, Phthiotians, Malians, Dolopians, Aenianians, Delphians, Phocians, as long as Aeschines allowed. Was this, then, not enough for disaster, but must there be added to it that the man who destroyed them should also hold what was theirs? And how much better to be one short of the number than to fill the place badly!

44. 'But they would not have listened to just arguments.' Perhaps they would have listened even to these, if not all, then some; for Philip had not, after all, courted them all; indeed, this very thing divided them most, that some had been well treated and others neglected. But even if justice had become worthless to all of them, yet fear, at least, [would have moved them], [of whether] it profited them to have a master set over their meetings in the guise of an Amphictyon. Do not suppose, men of Athens, that this is dangerous to your city but safe for the rest; the danger is equal for all. For terrible is the man's ambition, and his hatred of those who desire freedom. These considerations, then, would have persuaded them to admire nothing so much as to destroy themselves [for it].

But [you say] all speech is vain and much nonsense, and the one concern is that Philip should become an Amphictyon. Let him become one, Aeschines, but let him become one with the Athenians speaking against it. Let him win glory, but let us keep for ourselves the glory we have. Let him take on the Amphictyonic assembly too, but let it be seen [to happen] against the will of the Athenians.

Do not make a people in no way like the Thessalians an imitator of the Thessalians, nor one far different from the Thebans a copier of the Thebans. They gratify a barbarian. What wonder? They follow their fathers' examples. After earth, after water, after first-fruits of slavery, they have toasted away the Amphictyonic assembly. But for us there is no retreat; the wars fought for honour do not allow it, nor the trophies, some on land, some at sea, some at home, some abroad. Datis does not allow it, nor Xerxes, nor Mardonius, nor Masistius, nor the throne, nor the scimitar, nor Cyprus, nor Pamphylia. For to be born of good men would bring a strong compulsion to practise virtue.

And this too, Aeschines, I thought [should be put forward]: words of those men of old, from a *pylagoras*, fighting against a folly that gratifies barbarians. It would have been fine for later generations to hear this too, that every occasion found our ancestors good: occasions of war, of deeds, of speeches. But you, having kept silent there and disgraced them, blame the Amphictyons for your own baseness, though they surely did not stop your mouth.

48. "For I feared," he says, "that a war might come upon us from my words, and that so many cities, in their hostility, might make a joint campaign against our city." When you were destroying the Phocians, you did not fear then that you would make great the others who are hostile to the city.

But I let this pass; answer me this instead: would they have attacked us because they had long loved Philip and had complaints against us, and thought that the moment had now come, or because they were beginning their enmity from this point? For if they would gladly have retaliated against us even before, they had a sufficient occasion in Philip's wish, and there was no need to wait for what no one knew would happen. For if they had sent to Philip and asked him to lead them against us, saying they would readily follow and citing their numbers and their preparation, do you think he would have put it off to the next day, when he had his neighbours cowering, others destroyed, and these following him? He is not so idle, nor one who knows how to waste opportunities once given. But would they, while charging us with nothing else, have thought our great concern for the Amphictyonic assembly worth a war, they who, to escape the toils of war, look on while Greece is brought low and one man grows great?

If war were pleasant to the Greeks, and the practice of arms, and love of glory, and the training of bodies, it would also be a great thing for Philip to keep his present rule safe. But as it is they have cast out of their souls the ambition to strive in contests for justice, and, having hung up their shields, they sit listening to those who praise Philip, and they do not pity in the least the Greeks who are perishing, so that they may not be compelled to fight. From what change, then, would men who do not endure the necessary wars have chosen this one, to which no reasoning led?

Do you not see that those who most gratify Philip, the despicable Thessalians, have done so out of flight from war? They, so that Philip might fight the Phocians in their place, bought their respite at the price of slavery.

And even if the war against us were very easy, and campaigning and toiling painless for the Amphictyons, do you think they would have wished Athens not to exist? It is not so. Why? The future is uncertain, and the release from all misfortunes for everyone is this city, which both accuses and helps the same people. They know, then, that while you sit opposed to Philip, what saves them in hard times remains, but if you were destroyed, which may it not happen, the ground for their confidence would perish along with you. So even if they hated you intensely, they would still have held off, considering their own interest.

And indeed I cannot see even this, how they would have become hostile. For their favour to Philip, which they were most eager for, would have appeared no less even if opposition had come from you; rather, the favour would have become much greater because of the dispute. For it is a sign that what is given is no trifle when speeches are made arguing that it is not rightly given.

54. And why do I dwell on these things, leaving aside the strongest point? Our ancestors did not hand down to us this law, to consider the safest things best, but to consider what befits the city best even with dangers, and what is foreign to our character most terrible even with ease. The man who claims to manage public affairs must not frighten you, as one does children, nor make a tragedy of the sweat of war, but must consider this one thing terrible and hard: if you shun anything honourable for the sake of quiet.

Aeschines, I think, has been fortunate not to have lived in the time of the Persian Wars, for he would have felt the same then. What are you saying? "We would have been at war"? But did we not go to war for the rights of the Greeks, though we fell far short of the Lacedaemonians in resources? And recently did we not sail out for the Euboeans? Did we not send a force to the Olynthians? And hipparchs and taxiarchs are dear [to us]. What does this mean, Aeschines, not even enduring the name of war? As long as the city belongs to the Athenians, let it pray to live in peace, but let it accept wars for what is honourable, and let it regard the one as gentle, the other as necessary. Let this be said on the assumption that the Greeks would have made war; but that they would by no means have thrown themselves into such turmoil, I have just finished showing.

56. "But Philip," he says, "would certainly have attacked on his own." How can you say this, Aeschines? Did we not end the war? Were there not embassies? Have you not received the oaths? Slowly, and as suited Philip, but there is peace all the same, by your account. How then can there be war in peace? For we certainly did not agree to this as well, that he should share in the Amphictyony. And if he will always claim to gain something more because of the peace, I have no need of a peace harsher than war.

Would Philip have marched if we had spoken against it, but now that we have given him the Amphictyonic assembly, will he not do it when he is able? Of course, he will respect the treaty! Very much so: the Amphipolitans and the Pydnaeans could testify to this for you, the first of whom he slaughtered in the very midst of the oaths, while he drove out the others, those from whom he had received the city. Was he not at the same moment making excuses to the Olynthians and bringing up siege engines? Did he not destroy the Phocians while threatening the Thebans? Does he not, wherever he finds an opportunity for gain, mock the gods? From what war, then, did you free us by your silence?

58. One must always keep watch, men of Athens, and act so that Philip will not be able; for once he is able, there is nothing that will stop him. He will be great if you give way, but if you are awake and roused, he will be not only no greater than now, but not even as great as he is now. Let him remember the relief force sent to Thermopylae, which drove him back from the Phocians, and let him not be elated at present circumstances. For what is taken by deceit is not yet proof of the victor's strength.

But even if he is very strong in his foot-companions, who I hear know how to drink [rather] than to fight, a greater alliance, men of Athens, is the goodwill of the gods, and I for my part would rather take the field with these alone than with many tens of thousands. The Pythian himself, whose sacred place he defiles, would have given us himself and his alliance; Heracles, who is honoured somewhere there, our old fellow soldier; the goddess who obtained this land by lot, who walled the city with a wooden wall stronger than the Babylonian.

60. Bearing this in mind, Aeschines ought to have used the arguments available and proved our primacy over the other Greeks. Or rather, he was ignorant of none of this, but having sold his silence he was not going to speak. So he gratified [Philip] as much as the rest by saying nothing against it, for when someone who is present does not prevent shameful deeds as far as lies in him, he has acquired the reputation of an accomplice, since he who could have checked them and did not prevent them has done [the things] he allowed; and he was considering how Philip might not fail to gain membership and he himself might have some refuge with you.

How then? How could this be brought together? "Let the others speak, Philip, and praise your race, your policy, and your fortune; from me let silence suffice, which will give you the Amphictyonic assembly and me some argument at Athens." For he thinks you are already beaten in argument. You did not say that he should become one, but you did not speak against his becoming one. And this is both to make Philip an Amphictyon and to admit great fear. For you indicated that one ought to have spoken against it, but that it was necessary to be silent, and that Philip must think he obtained this from his own power, not from the Greeks. Have you done less wrong by keeping silent than if you had spoken in support?

62. "But you may speak against it," he says, "if you wish, and no one has taken this from you." I know that you want the opponents to appear and other *pylagorai* to go and denounce the matter, so that Philip may know more exactly how much you have conceded to him, and you may get, besides what you have received, a second fee.

But it does not undo your baseness if someone else should prove just, nor must our abundance of good citizens be a salvation for the wicked. For neither, if as general you saw the enemy's wall rotten, such as would fall at the first engine, and led the army away before taking it, would it serve you as a defence that those sent after you could take it. For if this saved the first man, it would save the second and the third and all in turn, and so the city would be full of men forever negligent, escaping [conviction] on the ground that they never attack but could take [the place] if they attacked.

But this is not a just *pylagoras*. Rather: if you yourself have left undone nothing of what was fitting, be saved; but if someone else is needed to do your part, may you die. We did not send this man out unwilling, nor shouting and protesting that he could not perform such services. For you do not compel anyone else either, men of Athens, of those who do not wish to manage your affairs; anyone who is called may decline, and there is no danger. But Aeschines, beforehand, promising that you would see him [act] as was fitting, and there were those who voted for him, who are present now too, to demand him [for punishment].

It is a common disgrace, men of Athens, that those entrusted with the greatest matters should be saved as a favour to others, when they have no [claim to it] from what they have done. Philip is an Amphictyon through the *pylagoras*, having inherited not his ancestral rank but that of the Phocians, who are hated by the Thebans because, when the Thebans demanded that our city be razed, the Phocians would not allow it. Philip is an Amphictyon, and a tyrant comes from Pella as a *hieromnemon*. What among the things thought novel has the sun looked upon before this? What land above the sea, what voyage across the mainland? Philip is an Amphictyon, and the council walled by ancient ordinance is thrown open to barbarians.

A king asked to share in the fellowship of the Greeks, a man licentious and insolent and an enemy of the Amphictyons, and one who thinks fit to wage wars to that end. And the descendant of a slave king, of Alexander who served as herald for Xerxes, sits and judges and casts his vote like an Athenian, like a Spartan. And that Alexander, though he was friendly to the Greeks and got his surname from that, neither asked nor hoped for anything so great; but this man, who on account of the very opposite is called the ruin of the Greeks, sits in state at Thermopylae, near the tomb of Leonidas.

Would the King believe this, if he heard it: that those who drove your forefather, who covered land and sea with his force, trembling out of Europe, and forced him to flee on a single ship, have laid aside that pride and do obeisance to Philip, while he crossed the Peneius, came through Thessaly, and, having made a great desolation around Thermopylae, has become one of the most genuine Greeks? If he heard this, would he not tear the informer apart as a deceiver? "What are you saying? Those who would not give a little water and a clod of earth have given the navel of the earth, as they themselves call it? And those who did not respect the law of heralds, when [the heralds] named him and proposed the yoke of slavery, and killed them, now crown Philip?"

Well, Aeschines has managed to bring this very thing about. Tell me, by the gods of our land, tell me: if, when you kept silent while these things were happening, envoys had suddenly appeared from Asia and said that the Great King, who has more arms than any other man, does not wish to take Greece as a slave, nor does he covet your trees or your other goods, but makes this one demand and thinks this one thing enviable, to be enrolled among the Amphictyons, would you have kept silent, or would you have been an orator? If you would have done the same, behold the *pylagoras*! But if you had at once spoken against them, what would you have said if someone asked: "Why do you put the slave before the master?" Or [would it be] that you have been in the company of the one, but not yet of the other?

69. There has never been, men of Athens, a harsher deed, nor one that showed more clearly that Greece is faring badly. I used to hear that Amphipolis had been taken: terrible, but it is in Thrace. I heard of Potidaea: colonists of the Athenians, but in Thrace. With such things I consoled myself about Pydna and Methone and all the rest: he snatched, he lied, he broke his oaths, he filched. These are the acts of a criminal, not a king, of some cutpurse, not a commander. But at what has happened now I choke as I look at your faces. Philip asked in broad daylight for so great a thing concerning Delphi, and did not fail, but has got it, with some speaking and one keeping silent.

O Deucalion and Amphictyon and Acrisius and Strophius and Eurylochus, it was not with these hopes that you founded, and you others renewed, the council that is now a laughing-stock! Again the Cirrhaeans, again the Acragallidae, or rather things far more terrible. For they, falling on those travelling to Pytho from outside, plundered whatever they could; but this man, not by harassing some sacred envoys or filching the silver or baggage of travellers, but [by taking] Olynthus and Methone and Apollonia and thirty-two cities, and by being the first to introduce the custom of cities being sold by those very men entrusted with them, has an honour [as reward] for his crimes and has become an Amphictyon.

And while each of the cities imposes punishments on the wicked, in the cities there is common praise for this polluted man, whom it does not befit even to approach the shrines of the Macedonians themselves, laden as he is with such defilement. Those who have prostituted themselves may not take part in sacred rites. Pammenes knows this man's youth in Thebes. And the Thebans, not ignorant of this, flatter him all the same. Murderers may not touch altars. But he began his bloodshed with his brothers, whom he kept driving out, slaughtering, and demanding [for surrender] until they were expelled.

Whoever moves a votive offering is at once led off and put to death. But Philip himself could not tell the number, not to say of the offerings, but even of the shrines [he has robbed]. For who has plundered so much? Who has razed? Who has burned? Who has made cities like uninhabited places, not attacking by the law of war, but mixing iron with friendship, arms with treaties, murders with oaths?

Consider how many tears there are now because of this man in many places on earth: of fathers for children, of children for fathers, of wives for husbands, wandering, begging, asking for alms, pitied, and not even having that. Consider what feelings those given to Atrestidas are likely to have, who are learning late in life to be slaves. The man who at dinner distributes the captives from Olynthus among the conjurors has received the Amphictyonic assembly as the prize of his cruelty.

74. And why do I speak of those elsewhere? Yesterday one of those who have fled here from there came up to me, having heard about the impeachment, and asked whether these things were true, and whether Philip was an Amphictyon, and whether with Aeschines keeping silent. And learning that both were so, he burst into tears and went away saying nothing. Such an Amphictyon has Aeschines made for us, one for whom it is not lawful even to look upon the Amphictyonic assembly, and he has filled the holiest of places with so much impurity.

Xerxes set foot on the Acropolis, but when the Athenians had abandoned the city, but hated him, but were at war with him, but fought him at sea, but would gladly have torn him apart. Philip, however, has been brought into the Amphictyonic assembly as a friend, as a good man, as pious, as just. Let him hold the place as an enemy, as a foe. With the Greeks absent, driven out, expelled, staying at home, let him hold it alone, let him judge alone; let him not be called a partner nor be a part of the ancient Amphictyons. I will bear the misfortune, but the favour I cannot bear.

76. And soon, men of Athens, he will sit alone. I know the man. He will not be content with the votes of the Phocians, nor will he endure seeing another vote prevailing, now agreeing with him, now opposing. He will find pretexts against those who meet with him, he will find other Phocians, he will again cut off a limb.

Nevertheless, even if he does his utmost to hold together, guard, and preserve those still surviving, at least the freedom for the others to meet and sit and speak and vote will be lost, and a dreadful inequality will take hold of the council, with him trailing the arrogance of tyranny and the others sinking into a humbler posture. And when the surrounding place is full of many horsemen, many hoplites, mercenaries, flatterers, cooks, a tent spangled with gold, and the rest of his retinue, perhaps someone will see there honoured even Callias, the man driven out from here, whom his character cast out of Athens but fitted to Philip.

78. For my part, men of Athens, may it not befall me to see the Amphictyonic assembly, nor Delphi, nor the Pythian games, when such a change has disturbed everything and such an upheaval has turned everything upside down. Dark is the spring, joyless the autumn, and the festival full of tears. And you, if you could go to Delphi through a deserted Phocis, would be men of iron. For one must lament, starting right from the borders as far as the temple, with no wall standing, no house remaining, no village of men to be seen, but only <old men and women and little children>.

Who will any longer choose, as *pylagoras*, to walk through so many evils to the man who wrought them with his own hand? Yours, Aeschines, is the task, the service suits your soul. You will travel in luxury, laughing, applauding. We see how much an envoy's wickedness can do. Or rather, why do I say this? Will you not put him to death? Will you not condemn him? Will you tolerate a voice that is nowhere to be seen on your behalf? On the stage he is loud-voiced, and at the purifications and in the religious bands, but wherever there is need to help the city, he is more voiceless than the shades.

Swiftly indeed would this man have imitated Cynegeirus or Codrus and given up his body for you, whether the god had ordained it by oracle or a battle pressed hard, he who for the sake of a few words did not defend his fatherland, nor reckoned with himself: 'Yet me, the son of Atrometus and Glaucothea, the man who marvelled at the fresh-kneaded cakes and the figs, the shameless tritagonist, the utterly wicked clerk, the people of the Athenians honoured as envoy, *pylagoras*, counsellor, and gave the finest things the democracy has.' But when he saw Philip and gold, he forgot everything.

Will you then let this man go? What ancestral virtue can he remind you of? What dedications? What trophies? What generalships? For my part I see none, unless these things deserve respect: his father's fetters, his mother's collar, this man's buskins, the wounds he got from the spectators, the shamelessness of Cyrebion and the whoring of Nicias. These, then, would help him more by being hidden than by being displayed. But about those engaged in politics I say this: let them stop making the city small and her enemies great, as though they would be better looked after in the greatness of the enemy.

82. And ask them this too: 'Would you, serving as *pylagoras*, have kept silent or not?' For you will find either that they are bad men and very like this one, or that they are accusers of Aeschines, who, having baited the people with the speeches he made in Arcadia, found greater rewards than he wished for, and once trusted, sold [them] out, speaking about the Phocians, but not speaking, now at the Amphictyonic assembly, and earlier in Macedonia, about Amphipolis. So long ago did he understand this manner of treason.

83. Will you not stop, men of Athens, putting the sinews of the city into the hands of these traffickers? Will you not, if you do not wish to put them to death, send them back to the stage and their former life, to Creon and Oenomaus, to Theodorus and Aristodemus, and set over your affairs men who look to Pericles?

Does a people that has Demosthenes of Paeania send out Aeschines of Cothocidae as *pylagoras*? They would not have withstood that man's spirit, nor his judgement, nor the stream of his words. He would have defeated the Thebans, overpowered the Thessalians, struck the rest with awe, and exposed the reputation of Python. But now you see what has happened: Aeschines is *pylagoras* and Philip an Amphictyon. Is there no missile, Apollo, from heaven, to imitate the peaks of Parnassus, which came rushing down from above and fell upon the barbarians, when the mountain sufficed in place of an army against the invaders?

But even if these things have not yet happened, many such must be expected. Great too was that famous Jason the Thessalian, both in his preparations and in his hopes, and he reached for the management of the Pythian games. But nevertheless, while these were near at hand, he lay dead, so much could seven men achieve.
